source: The Ideal Gas Law
PV = nRT = Nk_BT, with the temperature in kelvins.
Students use Celsius, so warming a gas from 20 °C to 40 °C seems to double its pressure.

In Kinetic Molecular Theory you met a gas as a swarm of tiny molecules flying in all directions, with pressure coming from their hits on the walls. Here that picture becomes one equation that ties together pressure $P$, volume $V$, temperature $T$ and the amount of gas. You will rearrange it often, as in Solving for a Variable.

Think about the hits on the walls. Twice as many molecules make twice as many hits, so $P \propto n$. Hotter molecules move faster, so they hit harder and more often, and the pressure grows in proportion to the absolute temperature. Give the same molecules twice the volume, and their hits spread over more wall and come less often, so $P \propto 1/V$. Put together, $P \propto nT/V$. The constant that makes it an equation is the gas constant $R$. The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, where this pressure would drop to zero; that is why the law needs kelvins.

$$\role{pressure}{P}\role{volume}{V} = \role[moles of gas]{amount}{n}\role[gas constant]{constant}{R}\role{temperature}{T} = \role[number of molecules]{amount}{N}\role[Boltzmann constant]{constant}{k_B}\role{temperature}{T}$$ with $P$ in pascals, $V$ in cubic meters, $T$ in kelvins ($T = T_C + 273$), $n$ in moles, $N$ the number of molecules, $R = 8.31\,\text{J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$ and $k_B = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\,\text{J/K}$.
Pressure is the average push of many tiny collisions. Try it in the Gas in a Box lab.
Worked examples
A $10.0\,\text{L}$ tank holds gas at $200\,\text{kPa}$ and $27\,^\circ\text{C}$. How many moles are inside?
How much gas?
$n = \dfrac{2000\,\text{J}}{2493\,\text{J/mol}} = 0.802\,\text{mol}$. (Pascals times cubic meters are joules.)
A sealed, rigid can of air at $150\,\text{kPa}$ warms from $20\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $40\,^\circ\text{C}$. What is the new pressure?
A warm can
$160\,\text{kPa}$
$n$ and $V$ are fixed, so $P/T$ is fixed: $P_2 = P_1 \dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$.
$P_2 = (150\,\text{kPa})\dfrac{313}{293} = 160\,\text{kPa}$, a rise of about $7\%$, not a doubling.
How many molecules are in $1.0\,\text{L}$ of air at $101\,\text{kPa}$ and $0\,^\circ\text{C}$?
Counting molecules
$2.7 \times 10^{22}$ molecules
Use the molecule form: $N = \dfrac{PV}{k_BT}$, with $V = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$ and $T = 273\,\text{K}$.

Using Celsius. Warming a gas from $20\,^\circ\text{C}$ to $40\,^\circ\text{C}$ does not double its pressure, because $40\,^\circ\text{C}$ is not twice as hot as $20\,^\circ\text{C}$: it is $313\,\text{K}$ against $293\,\text{K}$. Check: convert every temperature to kelvins before it goes into the gas law, and remember that a temperature of $0\,^\circ\text{C}$ would make $P = 0$ if Celsius were allowed.
Real gases follow $PV = nRT$ closely at everyday pressures and temperatures. It fails near the point where a gas condenses into a liquid, when the molecules' own size and attraction start to matter.
